title: Preface
summary: This is the third edition of a C++ textbook on data structures and algorithm analysis by Clifford A. Shaffer. It covers fundamental data structures (lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs), sorting and searching algorithms, file processing and external sorting, indexing, advanced data structures (tries, balanced trees, spatial structures), algorithm analysis techniques, lower bounds, patterns of algorithms (dynamic programming, randomized, numerical), limits to computation (NP-completeness, impossible problems), and includes mathematical preliminaries, exercises, projects, and an appendix. The book is freely available for non-commercial use, with copyright and contact details provided.

title: Preface

nodes.title: Approach:
nodes.summary: The preface argues for efficient programming despite advancing technology, emphasizing good design and algorithms over tricks. It outlines principles: costs/benefits, tradeoffs, avoiding reinventing the wheel, and matching data structures to needs. The book's approach covers techniques within these principles, with design patterns coverage increasing across editions. As a teaching text, it's for advanced data structures or algorithms courses, assuming programming experience in C++, recursion, and discrete math, with Chapter 2 reviewing prerequisites.

nodes.title: Using the Book in Class:
nodes.summary: This preface outlines the evolving role of design in data structures education, emphasizing principles like abstraction, common practices, and needs assessment. It details the textbook's evolution, from no design patterns to explicit coverage. The book targets teaching, not encyclopedic reference, covering most standard data structures and some new ones. It specifies course usage for sophomore to senior levels, recommends programming exercises, and notes prerequisites like programming and discrete math. Chapters' dependencies and 'Further Reading' sections are mentioned. C++ is used to illustrate concepts, focusing on ADT separation.

nodes.title: Use of C++:
nodes.summary: The preface outlines course structures for sophomore and senior levels using chapter selections, including advanced tree or dynamic structure assignments. It emphasizes flexibility in topic order and notes dependencies among chapters. It discusses the use of C++ for illustrating data structures, minimizing advanced features like inheritance and overloading, and mentions template usage. It distinguishes C++ implementations from pseudocode and addresses error handling via assertions. It stresses the necessity of programming exercises and analytical problems, providing over 450 exercises. Finally, it lists contact information and sources for supplementary materials, lecture notes, and code.

nodes.title: Exercises and Projects:
nodes.summary: The preface discusses using assertions for data structure conditions and exception handling, distinguishing tested C++ implementations from higher-level pseudocode. It emphasizes exercises and projects for learning data structures, including pointers, dynamic memory, recursion, design, and disk vs. memory access, noting over 450 exercises. It provides author contact details (email, mail) and supplementary materials: lecture notes, code examples, and course web pages.

nodes.title: 1 Data Structures and Algorithms
1 Data Structures and Algorithms (intro)
nodes.summary: The text introduces data structures and algorithms, showing how organizing information enables efficient answers to complex queries. It defines a data structure as any representation with operations, and states the book's three goals: presenting a toolkit of common data structures, introducing space-time tradeoffs, and teaching effectiveness measurement via asymptotic analysis. It contrasts algorithm design goals of clarity versus efficiency, mentions abstraction and design patterns, and previews a discussion on selecting data structures. It argues that increasing computing power does not reduce the need for efficiency, as problems grow more complex.

nodes.title: 1.1 A Philosophy of Data Structures
1.1.1 The Need for Data Structures
nodes.summary: This text discusses data structures and algorithms, emphasizing program elegance versus efficiency, with the book focusing on the latter via asymptotic analysis. It advocates a data-centered design philosophy: analyze problem operations, quantify resource constraints, then select the best data structure. It addresses why efficiency remains crucial despite better hardware, defines data structures, efficiency, and cost, and notes trade-offs. It outlines three key selection questions about insertion timing, deletion, and access patterns, and includes a bank account example balancing rapid transactions against slow account creation.

nodes.title: 1.1.2 Costs and Benefits
nodes.summary: The text discusses factors for choosing data structures: insertion timing, deletion support, and access order. It explains cost-benefit trade-offs, noting no universally best structure. Example 1.1 describes a bank needing fast exact-match search, efficient insertion, and low deletion priority, suggesting hash tables. Example 1.2 covers a city database requiring exact-match and range queries, rejecting hash tables for B+-trees or linear indexes. Section 1.2 defines data types (simple, aggregate, composite), data items, and distinguishes logical data types from physical implementations, using lists and arrays as examples.

This section presents a philosophy of data structures, emphasizing efficiency over program elegance through asymptotic analysis and a data-centered design approach. It outlines key selection factors: insertion timing, deletion support, and access order, and discusses cost-benefit trade-offs with no universally best structure. Examples include a bank account system (hash tables for fast exact-match search and insertion) and a city database (B+-trees or linear indexes for range queries). It also defines data types (simple, aggregate, composite), data items, and distinguishes logical data types from physical implementations.

nodes.title: 1.2 Abstract Data Types and Data Structures
nodes.summary: The text discusses efficient range query processing in databases, comparing hash tables, B+-trees, and linear indexes. It introduces data types, distinguishing simple vs. aggregate types, data items, and logical vs. physical forms. Abstract Data Types (ADTs) are defined as software components with encapsulated interfaces, while data structures are their implementations. Examples illustrate ADTs for integers, lists, and cars. The text emphasizes abstraction for managing complexity, and design patterns as reusable, high-level abstractions for program design, akin to templates that generalize recurring design solutions.

nodes.title: 1.3 Design Patterns
1.3 Design Patterns (intro)
nodes.summary: This text explains the relationship between data items, abstract data types (ADTs), and data structures, noting that ADTs define logical form while data structures implement physical form. It introduces design patterns as reusable solutions for recurring design problems, aimed at transferring expert knowledge and improving communication. Two specific patterns are described: Flyweight, which reduces memory cost by sharing identical object information (e.g., character objects in document layout or empty nodes in PR quadtrees), and Visitor, mentioned as an activity applied to every node in a tree traversal, such as counting nodes in a page layout tree.

nodes.title: 1.3.1 Flyweight
nodes.summary: The text introduces design pattern variations and presents two simple patterns: Flyweight and Visitor. Flyweight reduces memory cost by sharing identical object information, illustrated with document character representations and PR quadtree empty leaf nodes. Visitor is mentioned as a pattern for performing activities on tree nodes, referencing tree traversal for counting nodes, though not fully detailed.

nodes.title: 1.3.2 Visitor
nodes.summary: This section introduces design patterns: Flyweight, Visitor, and Composite. Flyweight reduces memory by sharing identical object representations, illustrated with document characters and PR quadtree leaf nodes. Visitor enables generic tree traversal with pluggable activities, used in tree and graph traversal. Composite compares procedural and object-oriented approaches for applying actions to hierarchies of objects, discussing tradeoffs between adding activities versus object types in page layout composition.

nodes.title: 1.3.3 Composite
nodes.summary: The text discusses three design patterns: Visitor, which uses generic traversal with activities passed as parameters; Composite, contrasting procedural versus object-oriented hierarchy handling, where subclasses embody actions for frequent object type additions; and Strategy, encapsulating interchangeable actions like rendering for different devices. It compares Composite vs. Visitor based on traversal control, and distinguishes Visitor vs. Strategy by intent and focus, noting both pass activities but differ in substitution versus application across nodes, including examples from sections on tree and graph traversal, page composition, and sorting.

nodes.title: 1.3.4 Strategy
nodes.summary: The text discusses design patterns: Composite (burying functional activity in subclasses for easy new object addition) and Strategy (encapsulating interchangeable actions, e.g., rendering strategies). It contrasts Composite, Visitor, and Strategy patterns, highlighting subtle differences in intent. Then it defines problems, algorithms, and programs: problems as tasks with inputs/outputs and resource constraints, instances, and deterministic functions. It clarifies that all program outputs are fully determined by inputs, addressing apparent randomness like the UNIX date command.

This section introduces design patterns as reusable solutions for recurring design problems, explaining the relationship between data items, ADTs, and data structures. It details four patterns: Flyweight, which reduces memory by sharing identical object information (e.g., document characters, PR quadtree leaf nodes); Visitor, enabling generic tree traversal with pluggable activities; Composite, comparing procedural and object-oriented hierarchy handling and tradeoffs between adding activities versus object types; and Strategy, encapsulating interchangeable actions like rendering. It contrasts these patterns based on intent and traversal control, then defines problems, algorithms, programs, and instances, clarifying that program outputs are fully determined by inputs despite apparent randomness.

nodes.title: 1.4 Problems, Algorithms, and Programs
nodes.summary: This text distinguishes problems, algorithms, and programs. Problems are tasks defined by inputs and outputs, with resource constraints, acting as mathematical functions. Algorithms are methods to solve problems, requiring correctness, concrete steps, unambiguous next steps, finite steps, and termination. Programs are concrete implementations of algorithms in programming languages; not all programs are algorithms due to termination requirements. The text also includes a further reading list on data structures and algorithms, citing works by Knuth, Sedgewick, Manber, Cormen et al., and Skiena.

nodes.title: 1.5 Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text covers iteration in programming and algorithm termination. It distinguishes algorithms from programs, noting that programs may not terminate but algorithms must, and defines problems, algorithms, and programs. It lists further readings on data structures, algorithms, problem-solving, C++ programming, and design patterns. It also introduces chapter exercises on slow programs, integer representations, ADTs for strings and lists, and integer variable representation.

nodes.title: 1.6 Exercises
nodes.summary: The text covers design pattern references, including the 'gang of four' book, and lists 20 exercises from a data structures chapter. Exercises explore slow programs, arbitrary-precision integers, ADTs for strings/lists/2D arrays, integer representation, generalizing sorting and searching, algorithm existence, spelling checker design, database implementations, searching sorted arrays, comparing sorting algorithms, parenthesis balancing, graph representations, sorting invoices and arrays, finding max/second largest/middle values, and achieving O(log n) insertion and search.

This section introduces data structures and algorithms, defining data structures as representations with operations and outlining goals: presenting a toolkit, space-time tradeoffs, and asymptotic analysis. It contrasts clarity versus efficiency, emphasizes abstraction and design patterns, and argues efficiency remains crucial as problems grow. It covers data structure philosophy, selection factors, and examples like hash tables and B+-trees. It distinguishes problems, algorithms, and programs, including termination requirements. Finally, it provides further reading and exercises on various topics.

nodes.title: 2 Mathematical Preliminaries
2.1 Sets and Relations
nodes.summary: This chapter covers mathematical preliminaries: set notation, operations (union, intersection, difference), powersets, bags, sequences, and relations. It defines relation properties (reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive), equivalence relations, partitions, partial orders, total orders, and provides examples. It also introduces miscellaneous notation for units of measure (bytes, bits, KB, MB, GB, ms), the factorial function, Stirling's approximation, and permutations, including a method for generating random permutations. Estimation is highlighted as a useful engineering skill for discarding infeasible solutions early.

nodes.title: 2.2 Miscellaneous Notation
nodes.summary: This text covers several mathematical preliminaries: partial orders via subset relations, units of measure (bytes, bits, KB, MB, GB, ms) with power-of-two vs decimal distinctions, the factorial function and Stirling's approximation, permutations including a C++ random permutation function, Boolean variables and logic notation (implication, equivalence, and, or, not), floor and ceiling functions, modulus operator with divergence between mathematical and programming definitions (especially for negative numbers), and logarithms including base-2 usage, properties, and applications like binary search.

nodes.title: 2.3 Logarithms
nodes.summary: The text addresses issues with modulo in hash functions, requiring positive results. It defines logarithms, highlighting base 2 usage in programming with examples for minimum bits for n codes and binary search halving. It lists logarithmic properties: product, quotient, power, and base change, noting constant factor differences and that base is often ignored asymptotically. It explains notations like log^2 n, log log n, and log* n with an example. Finally, it introduces summations and Sigma notation for summing costs in loop analysis.

nodes.title: 2.4 Summations and Recurrences
nodes.summary: The text covers logarithm properties, including multiplication, division, power rules, base change, and notation like log^2 n and log* n. It introduces summations and recurrences, explaining Sigma notation, closed-form solutions, and listing useful summations. It defines recurrence relations with examples like factorial and Fibonacci, demonstrating expansion to find patterns. Recursion is discussed, emphasizing base cases and recursive calls, with examples including a recursive factorial function and the Towers of Hanoi puzzle.

nodes.title: 2.5 Recursion
nodes.summary: This text covers recursion in algorithms. It defines recursive algorithms with base cases and recursive calls, illustrating with a C++ factorial function. It discusses the Towers of Hanoi puzzle, providing a recursive solution with multiple calls, and contrasts recursion with iteration, noting recursion's inefficiency due to function calls but its utility in simplifying design, especially for recursive data structures like trees. Additionally, it introduces mathematical proof techniques, emphasizing the importance of both investigation and argument phases, and the role of standard proof structures in technical writing.

nodes.title: 2.6 Mathematical Proof Techniques
2.6 Mathematical Proof Techniques (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers recursion using the Tower of Hanoi algorithm, noting its primary use in simplifying algorithm design despite inefficiency, and its natural fit for recursive data structures and divide-and-conquer algorithms. It then discusses mathematical proof techniques, emphasizing investigation and argument phases, and introduces three methods: direct proof (logical deduction), proof by contradiction (assuming falsehood to derive a contradiction), with an example proving there is no largest integer.

nodes.title: 2.6.1 Direct Proof
nodes.summary: This section introduces three mathematical proof techniques: direct proof, proof by contradiction, and proof by mathematical induction. Direct proof, also called deduction, is a logical argument often expressed as "if...then" (P ⇒ Q) and can use logical equivalences. Proof by contradiction involves assuming the theorem is false and deriving a contradiction to conclude it is true, illustrated by the example proving there is no largest integer via assuming a largest integer B and considering B+1. Mathematical induction is mentioned but not detailed here.

nodes.title: 2.6.2 Proof by Contradiction
nodes.summary: This section introduces three common proof techniques: direct proof (logical deduction, often using "if...then" or P⇒Q, with examples like proving equivalence via both directions), proof by contradiction (assuming the theorem false to derive a contradiction, illustrated by proving there is no largest integer, and noting the related contrapositive), and proof by mathematical induction (defining base case and induction step, including strong induction, and linking induction to recursion and algorithm analysis for proving hypotheses about summations or recurrences).

nodes.title: 2.6.3 Proof by Mathematical Induction
nodes.summary: The text covers mathematical proof techniques, focusing on proof by contradiction and mathematical induction. It explains induction's base case and induction step, including strong induction, and draws parallels between induction, recursion, and algorithm design. It presents multiple examples: proving summation formulas, recurrence relations, stamp combinations, prime divisibility, two-coloring regions formed by lines, and correctness of a recursive factorial function, emphasizing termination proofs. The section also introduces estimation techniques, including a three-step process for back-of-the-envelope calculations, and an example estimating library bookcase requirements.

This section covers mathematical proof techniques and recursion. It begins with recursion using the Tower of Hanoi, highlighting its algorithmic design utility and fit for recursive data structures and divide-and-conquer. Three proof methods are introduced: direct proof (logical deduction, often using P⇒Q), proof by contradiction (assuming falsehood to derive a contradiction, with the example that no largest integer exists), and mathematical induction (base case and induction step, including strong induction, linked to recursion and algorithm analysis). Examples include proving summation formulas, recurrence relations, stamp combinations, prime divisibility, two-coloring regions, and recursive factorial correctness. Estimation techniques with a three-step process are also presented.

nodes.title: 2.7 Estimation
nodes.summary: The text covers estimation techniques in computer science, including a three-step process, the importance of unit consistency, error bounds, and cross-verification. It provides examples: estimating library bookcases for one million pages, comparing car fuel efficiency with a higher purchase price, and estimating grocery costs. Finally, it lists further readings in discrete mathematics and related resources.

nodes.title: 2.8 Further Reading
nodes.summary: This text covers estimation examples: calculating library bookcase capacity using rough estimates, comparing car fuel economy with a price difference and payback period, and estimating supermarket totals by rounding prices. It lists further readings in discrete mathematics, algorithms, recursion, proof techniques, problem-solving, and estimation, including works by Epp, Graham et al., Manber, Roberts, Friedman and Felleisen, Solow, Zeitz, Bentley, and Gleick. Finally, it presents exercises on relation properties (reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive) and equivalence relations for various definitions.

nodes.title: 2.9 Exercises
nodes.summary: This text covers Chapter 2 exercises and preliminaries from an algorithms textbook. It includes references for mathematical induction, recursion, proof techniques, and estimation, plus exercises on relations (properties, equivalence, partial orders), ADTs for sets, bags, and sequences, recursive and iterative algorithms (factorial, Fibonacci, Towers of Hanoi, permutations, subsets, LCF), proofs (prime infinitude, irrationality, summations, Pigeonhole Principle), recurrence relations, probability, and estimation problems. It ends with an introduction to Chapter 3 on asymptotic algorithm analysis, growth rates, upper/lower bounds, and cost distinctions.

This section covers mathematical preliminaries essential for algorithm analysis. It introduces set theory, relations (properties, equivalence, partial orders), and notation for units, factorials, Stirling's approximation, and permutations. It details Boolean logic, floor/ceiling, modulus, and logarithms with properties and applications. Summations and recurrences are explained with Sigma notation, closed forms, and examples like factorial and Fibonacci. Recursion is defined with base cases, recursive calls, and examples (factorial, Towers of Hanoi), contrasting with iteration. Mathematical proof techniques—direct proof, contradiction, and induction (including strong induction)—are presented with examples. Estimation techniques with a three-step process and examples are included. The section concludes with further readings and exercises on relations, ADTs, algorithms, proofs, recurrences, probability, and estimation, leading into asymptotic analysis.

nodes.title: 3 Algorithm Analysis
3.1 Introduction
nodes.summary: This chapter introduces algorithm analysis, focusing on asymptotic analysis to estimate resource consumption and compare algorithm efficiency. It covers growth rates, upper and lower bounds, and the distinction between algorithm cost and problem cost. It discusses basic operations, input size, and running time functions, using examples like largest-value sequential search, constant time, and quadratic time. It presents growth rate graphs and tables, and explains best, worst, and average cases for algorithms such as sequential search, noting practical difficulties in empirical measurement and principles for code tuning.

nodes.title: 3.2 Best, Worst, and Average Cases
nodes.summary: This text discusses algorithm analysis, focusing on best, worst, and average cases. It illustrates these using factorial calculation and sequential search, explaining how input variation affects running time. The best case is rarely useful, while worst-case analysis ensures performance guarantees, crucial for real-time systems. Average-case analysis depends on input distribution and may not always be feasible. The text also addresses whether a faster computer or a better algorithm is preferable, noting that faster hardware often leads to solving larger problems rather than reducing time for the same problem.

nodes.title: 3.3 A Faster Computer, or a Faster Algorithm?
nodes.summary: This text discusses algorithm analysis: worst-case for real-time vs. average-case analysis requiring input distribution knowledge, else worst-case. It examines how a ten times faster computer affects problem size for various growth rates (linear, quadratic, n log n, exponential), showing constant factors don't affect relative improvement; exponential growth yields only additive increases. It advocates replacing quadratic with n log n algorithms over faster hardware when problem size exceeds a threshold. Asymptotic analysis ignores constant factors to focus on growth rate, useful except for small n or large constants. It introduces upper bounds.

nodes.title: 3.4 Asymptotic Analysis
3.4.1 Upper Bounds
nodes.summary: This text introduces asymptotic analysis for comparing algorithm growth rates, ignoring constant factors because they only shift curve intersection points and computer speed changes scale problem size uniformly. It defines big-Oh (O) for upper bounds with formal definition and examples, emphasizing tightest bounds, input class context, and limitations for small n or large constants. It then introduces big-Omega (Ω) for lower bounds with its symmetric definition.

nodes.title: 3.4.2 Lower Bounds
nodes.summary: The text discusses asymptotic analysis, explaining that algorithm growth rates depend on input cases: best, average, or worst. It introduces Big-Oh for upper bounds, Big-Omega for lower bounds, and Big-Theta when both bounds match within a constant factor. Examples include sequential search and functions like T(n) = c1n2 + c2n. It emphasizes choosing tight bounds and clarifies notation, noting that Big-Oh is not strict equality. It also mentions an alternate Big-Omega definition for cases where lower bound occurs infinitely often, and concludes that asymptotic notations are modeling tools, not laws of nature.

nodes.title: 3.4.3  Notation
nodes.summary: This text covers asymptotic analysis, focusing on Ω and Θ notations. It defines Ω, illustrates it with T(n)=c1n2+c2n and a pathological case, and introduces Θ when upper and lower bounds match. It compares Θ with big-Oh, noting limitations and preferences. Finally, it presents four simplifying rules for deriving asymptotic expressions from running-time equations.

nodes.title: 3.4.4 Simplifying Rules
nodes.summary: This text covers asymptotic analysis, emphasizing Θ notation over big-Oh when upper and lower bounds match, and noting cases lacking Θ analysis. It details simplifying rules: transitivity, ignoring constants, summing costs via max, and multiplying costs for loops, applicable to O, Ω, and Θ. It also describes classifying functions by limit ratios to determine growth rates, with an example comparing 2n log n and n2.

nodes.title: 3.4.5 Classifying Functions
nodes.summary: The text covers algorithm analysis rules for simplifying cost functions using Big-Oh, Omega, and Theta notations, including ignoring constants and lower-order terms, and summing costs of sequential code. It explains classifying functions by comparing growth rates via limits, with an example. It then demonstrates calculating running time for code fragments: constant-time assignment, a simple for loop, and nested loops, showing how to derive asymptotic costs like Θ(1), Θ(n), and Θ(n^2).

This section covers asymptotic analysis for comparing algorithm growth rates, ignoring constant factors. It defines big-Oh for upper bounds, big-Omega for lower bounds, and big-Theta for tight bounds, with formal definitions and examples. It discusses input classes (best, average, worst), choosing tightest bounds, limitations for small n or large constants, and an alternate big-Omega definition. It presents simplifying rules: transitivity, ignoring constants, summing costs via max, and multiplying costs for loops, applicable to O, Ω, and Θ. It also covers classifying functions by limit ratios to determine growth rates, with examples and running time analysis of code fragments, concluding that asymptotic notations are modeling tools.

nodes.title: 3.5 Calculating the Running Time for a Program
nodes.summary: Section 3.5 analyzes running times of code fragments: constant assignment, linear loops, nested loops yielding quadratic or n log n time, and binary search with logarithmic complexity, contrasting it with linear sequential search. It discusses control statements (while, if, switch), subroutine calls, and recursive functions via recurrence relations. The section also covers average-case analysis and amortized analysis. Section 3.6 introduces analyzing problems, defining upper and lower bounds, using sorting as an example to illustrate the gap between Ω(n) and O(n^2), and mentioning O(n log n) algorithms.

nodes.title: 3.6 Analyzing Problems
nodes.summary: This text covers analyzing problems using algorithm analysis, defining upper and lower bounds for problems, and the challenge of proving lower bounds. It uses sorting as an example, discussing its Ω(n) lower bound, O(n²) upper bound from simple algorithms, O(n log n) algorithms, and the proof that sorting is Θ(n log n). It also addresses common misunderstandings in asymptotic analysis, emphasizing the distinction between upper/lower bounds and best/worst/average cases, and the role of Θ-notation with incomplete knowledge.

nodes.title: 3.7 Common Misunderstandings
nodes.summary: This text covers common misunderstandings in asymptotic analysis, emphasizing that upper/lower bounds describe growth rates of cost measures, not best/worst cases, and that Θ-notation indicates matching bounds. It explains that best/worst cases exist for each input size, illustrated with sequential search and maximum-finding examples. It also introduces multiple-parameter analysis using a pixel-counting algorithm, showing its cost depends on both the number of pixels (P) and colors (C), with total time Θ(P log P) due to sorting.

nodes.title: 3.8 Multiple Parameters
nodes.summary: The text discusses time complexity analysis for algorithms with multiple parameters and space bounds. It explains sequential search cost variations in best, average, and worst cases, emphasizing the need for specifying input class. Using a pixel-ranking algorithm, it shows how cost analysis requires multiple parameters, yielding Θ(P + C log C), and argues against using only one variable. Finally, it introduces space bounds, comparing space analysis to time analysis, with examples: an array of n integers requiring Θ(n) space and a friendship matrix requiring Θ(n^2) space.

nodes.title: 3.9 Space Bounds
nodes.summary: The text explains algorithm cost analysis using pixels and colors, advocating Θ(P + C log C) rather than Θ(P log P) or Θ(C log C). It introduces space bounds, examples for arrays and friendship graphs, overhead, and the space/time tradeoff principle with lookup tables and Binsort in-place sorting. It contrasts disk-based tradeoffs, where smaller storage yields faster programs, and notes that growth rate differences like Θ(n log n) versus Θ(n²) matter greatly, mentioning sorting and searching.

nodes.title: 3.10 Speeding Up Your Programs
nodes.summary: The text discusses in-place sorting with Θ(n) time and space tradeoffs, contrasting main memory and disk-based principles. It covers speeding up programs through algorithm improvements versus code tuning, emphasizing focusing on key code, using profilers, avoiding work, and not hindering compiler optimizations. Examples include bounding box tests and Selection Sort. Finally, it addresses empirical analysis limitations, comparative timing pitfalls, and simulation as an alternative analytic method, illustrated with hash table analysis.

nodes.title: 3.11 Empirical Analysis
nodes.summary: This text covers empirical analysis as an alternative to asymptotic analysis, highlighting its limitations and pitfalls like code-tuning bias and experimental errors. It discusses simulation for complex problems, referencing hash table cost analysis. Further reading includes pioneering works by Knuth, Aho, and others, notes on algorithm efficiency, and coding improvements. Exercises ask for efficiency ranges, graphing, and ordering expressions by growth rate, including using Stirling's approximation for n!.

nodes.title: 3.12 Further Reading
nodes.summary: Section 3.12 lists pioneering algorithm analysis works by Knuth, Aho et al., and others, noting the origin of notation and a numerical analysis complexity reduction. It cites efficiency gains from coding, binary search bug history, and references for further reading. Section 3.13 provides exercises: finding efficient n ranges for expressions from Figure 3.1, graphing expressions to determine efficiency ranges, and ordering expressions by growth rate, including n! with Stirling's approximation.

nodes.title: 3.13 Exercises
nodes.summary: This chapter section on algorithm analysis covers further reading, including pioneering works by Knuth, Aho, Hopcroft, and Ullman, and alternate definitions; discusses notation and algorithm efficiency, citing Bentley's numerical analysis example and Brooks on programmer efficiency; and lists exercises on big-Oh, Omega, Theta, growth rates, binary search modifications, and algorithm design. Exercises include determining efficient ranges, graphing expressions, arranging by growth rate, analyzing hardware speedup, proving properties, finding bounds, and modifying binary search for duplicates, predecessors, infinite arrays, and different dividing points. Projects include comparing Boolean storage types.

nodes.title: 3.14 Projects
nodes.summary: The text covers algorithm analysis exercises: finding n in O(log n) comparisons, modifying binary search dividing points (l+(r-l)/3 and r-2) to analyze worst-case time and constant factors, designing a jigsaw puzzle assembly algorithm with a compare function and runtime summation, questioning average case vs. worst/best case costs, proving average case Θ implies worst case Ω and best case O, and projects on Boolean value access timing, sequential vs. binary search timing, and Fibonacci function timing.

This section covers algorithm analysis, focusing on asymptotic analysis, growth rates, and bounds (big-Oh, big-Omega, big-Theta). It explains best, worst, and average cases; compares faster hardware versus better algorithms; and details running time calculation for code including loops, recursion, and amortized analysis. It discusses analyzing problems, common misunderstandings, multiple parameters, space bounds, and speeding up programs via algorithm improvements and code tuning. Empirical analysis, simulation, further reading, exercises, and projects are also included.

nodes.title: 4 Lists, Stacks, and Queues
4 Lists, Stacks, and Queues (intro)
nodes.summary: This chapter covers lists, stacks, and queues, starting with the list ADT—a finite, ordered sequence of elements with operations for insertion, removal, access, creation, and clearing. It highlights separating logical representation (ADT) from physical implementation and uses asymptotic analysis for simple operations. It introduces dictionaries and compares array-based and linked list implementations. Sections cover the list ADT, stacks, queues with sample implementations, and the Dictionary ADT, setting the stage for search structures like binary search trees.

nodes.title: 4.1 Lists
4.1 Lists (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers list definitions as finite ordered sequences, emphasizing position and current position concept. It details the list ADT with operations like insert, remove, clear, moveToStart, next, prev, and getValue, using C++ abstract class and template. It discusses empty lists, length, head, tail, unsorted lists, and notation. nodes.title: 4.1.1 Array-Based List Implementation

nodes.title: Freelists

nodes.title: 4.1.3 Comparison of List Implementations

Space efficiency depends on n, P, E, and D, with formulas DE for array-based and n(P+E) for linked lists, the smaller determining the more efficient implementation for n elements.

nodes.title: 4.1.3 Comparison of List Implementations
nodes.summary: The text covers the static freelist declaration and its per-type implications, then compares array-based and linked list implementations in terms of space efficiency, access time, and insertion/deletion costs, including break-even formulas and dynamic arrays with amortized analysis. nodes.title: 5 Binary Trees

5.1 Definitions and Properties (intro)

nodes.title: 5.1.1 The Full Binary Tree Theorem
nodes.summary: The text covers Section 5.1 on binary tree definitions and properties, including full and complete binary trees, with examples. nodes.title: 5.1.2 A Binary Tree Node ADT

nodes.title: 5.2 Binary Tree Traversals

nodes.title: 5.4 Binary Search Trees

nodes.title: 5.6.3 Search in Huffman Trees

Section 6.6 lists further readings on tree implementations and union/find algorithms, and Section 6.7 provides exercises on tree algorithms, weighted union, path compression, and height union.

nodes.title: 6.6 Further Reading
nodes.summary: This text covers further reading references on Ackermann's function, path compression, and disjoint set union, including Tarjan's and Galil & Italiano's works, plus Samet's book on multidimensional tree structures. It then presents exercises: algorithms to check if general or binary trees are identical (with or without subtree ordering), postorder traversal for general trees, counting nodes using GenTree and GTNode ADTs, implementing weighted union efficiently with node modifications, comparing height union to weighted union, and simulating weighted union with path compression on an array.

nodes.title: 6.7 Exercises
nodes.summary: This covers further reading on Ackermann's function and disjoint set union, plus exercises and projects on general trees. Exercises include algorithms for tree identity, postorder traversal, node counting, weighted and height union rules, path compression and halving, equivalence class simulations, space efficiency analysis, K-ary tree properties, sequential representations, and decoding functions. Projects involve implementing general tree classes with various representations, a BST file archiver, and using UNION/FIND for clustering.

nodes.title: 6.8 Projects
nodes.summary: Exercises on decoding sequential representations for full binary and general trees, devising a Huffman coding tree representation, and project tasks: implementing general tree classes with left-child/right-sibling and child pointer arrays (fixed and dynamic), a BST file archiver, UNION/FIND for point clustering with complexity analysis, and empirical tests comparing five path compression variations in UNION/FIND.

Section 6 covers non-binary trees. It defines general trees, terminology, and an ADT for general tree nodes, including preorder and postorder traversals. The parent pointer implementation is presented for disjoint sets and UNION/FIND operations, with optimizations like weighted union and path compression. General tree implementations include lists of children, left-child/right-sibling representations, and dynamic nodes. K-ary trees are defined with examples and properties. Sequential implementations using minimal structural information are discussed for space efficiency. Further readings and exercises cover algorithms, implementations, and optimizations. Projects involve implementing tree classes, a file archiver, and clustering using UNION/FIND.
