nodes.title: 7 Internal Sorting
7 Internal Sorting (intro)
nodes.summary: This chapter introduces internal sorting, covering its importance, everyday examples, and computational applications. It outlines multiple algorithm design approaches like divide-and-conquer (Mergesort, Quicksort, Radix Sort) and analysis techniques such as average vs. worst-case and tuning. It previews algorithms with Θ(n²), Θ(n log n), and Θ(n) times, and a lower bound proof for Ω(n log n). It defines sorting terminology, notation, records, comparators, the sorting problem, stability, and mentions comparing algorithms via timing.

nodes.title: 7.1 Sorting Terminology and Notation
nodes.summary: The chapter covers internal sorting algorithms for records in main memory. It outlines three simple Θ(n²) algorithms (average/worst cases), then presents faster Θ(n log n) worst-case methods, and a special-case Θ(n) sort, concluding with a proof that sorting generally requires Ω(n log n) worst-case time. Sorting terminology and notation are defined: records stored in arrays, compared via a comparator class with a prior method, swapped via a swap function; the sorting problem requires non-decreasing key order, allowing duplicates. Stability (preserving duplicate order) is discussed. Comparison of algorithms is cautioned due to input-dependent running times; analysis typically measures key comparisons or swaps, assuming constant-time operations, but special situations (variable-length keys, frequent small sorts, memory constraints) matter. Section 7.2 introduces three simple sorting algorithms, starting with Insertion Sort, which iteratively inserts each record into a growing sorted list.

nodes.title: 7.2 Three (n2) Sorting Algorithms
7.2.1 Insertion Sort
nodes.summary: The text discusses factors affecting sorting algorithm performance, such as input size, key characteristics, and record movement, and traditional measures like comparisons and swaps. It introduces three Θ(n²) sorting algorithms, focusing on Insertion Sort with its C++ implementation, step-by-step process, and complexity analysis covering best, worst, and average cases, including inversion counting. Bubble Sort is briefly introduced as slow and inefficient, with a simple double loop design that inspires a later better algorithm.

nodes.title: 7.2.2 Bubble Sort
nodes.summary: The text covers three Θ(n²) sorting algorithms: Insertion Sort, Bubble Sort, and Selection Sort. For Insertion Sort, it analyzes best-case Θ(n), worst-case Θ(n²), and average-case Θ(n²) costs, explaining inversions, comparisons, and swaps. Bubble Sort, described as slow with poor best-case performance, uses adjacent swaps and always makes Θ(n²) comparisons, with swaps equal to Insertion Sort. Selection Sort repeatedly selects the smallest remaining element, requiring Θ(n²) comparisons but only n−1 swaps. C++ implementations and illustrative figures are provided for each algorithm.

nodes.title: 7.2.3 Selection Sort
nodes.summary: Section 7.2.3 covers Selection Sort, explaining its method of selecting the ith smallest key, with a C++ implementation and comparison to Bubble Sort, noting fewer swaps and advantages for large records. It includes an illustrative figure. Section 7.2.4 discusses the cost of exchange sorts (Insertion, Bubble, Selection), summarizing their comparisons and swaps across best, average, and worst cases, explaining their Θ(n2) running time due to adjacent comparisons. It also mentions the pointer-swapping technique to reduce swap costs and includes figures and a footnote on Selection Sort's swap anomaly.

nodes.title: 7.2.4 The Cost of Exchange Sorting
nodes.summary: The text covers swapping pointers to records to reduce swap costs, using Figure 7.4 to illustrate. It then discusses the cost of exchange sorts (Insertion, Bubble, Selection), comparing their best, average, and worst-case comparisons and swaps in Figure 7.5, and explains that these algorithms are Θ(n²) due to comparing only adjacent records. It analyzes inversions to show exchange sorts require at least Ω(n²) average time. Finally, it introduces Shellsort, its strategy, use of non-adjacent comparisons, and sublist sorting.

Section 7.2 covers three Θ(n²) sorting algorithms: Insertion Sort, Bubble Sort, and Selection Sort. It discusses factors affecting performance, including input size, key characteristics, and record movement, using comparisons and swaps as measures. For each algorithm, it provides C++ implementations and complexity analyses: Insertion Sort (best Θ(n), worst/average Θ(n²)), Bubble Sort (always Θ(n²) comparisons, swaps similar to Insertion Sort), and Selection Sort (Θ(n²) comparisons, n−1 swaps). It compares their costs across best, average, and worst cases, explains their Ω(n²) average time due to adjacent comparisons, and introduces pointer swapping to reduce swap costs. Shellsort is briefly introduced.

nodes.title: 7.3 Shellsort
nodes.summary: The text compares asymptotic complexities of insertion, bubble, and selection sorts using a figure, then discusses inversions to show adjacent-comparison sorts are Ω(n²) on average. It introduces Shellsort, explaining its diminishing increment strategy, virtual sublists, and Insertion Sort passes, illustrated with a 16-element example and C++ code. It notes Shellsort works with any increments ending in 1, recommends division-by-three increments for O(n^1.5) average performance, and concludes that Shellsort exploits Insertion Sort's best case, performing well for medium n. Finally, it introduces Mergesort via divide and conquer.

nodes.title: 7.4 Mergesort
nodes.summary: The text covers Shellsort with code, increments, and O(n^1.5) average performance, then Mergesort: its divide-and-conquer approach, merge function, linked list suitability, array implementation challenges, standard and optimized implementations, and Θ(n log n) analysis for all cases. It concludes by introducing Quicksort as an alternative divide-and-conquer strategy.

nodes.title: 7.5 Quicksort
nodes.summary: This text covers Mergesort and Quicksort. Mergesort's optimized implementation uses Insertion Sort for small subarrays and sentinel-based merging, with Θ(n log n) complexity in all cases. Quicksort is introduced as a space-efficient, fast average-case algorithm that partitions around a pivot, with worst-case Θ(n²) and best/average Θ(n log n). Pivot selection, partitioning, and optimizations like median-of-three, small-subarray cutoff, and recursion elimination are discussed. The text concludes by introducing Heapsort, which uses a balanced heap structure for Θ(n log n) performance in all cases, and is suitable for large datasets.

nodes.title: 7.6 Heapsort
nodes.summary: Covers Quicksort optimization via subarray bounds, stack depth care, and inlining; introduces Heapsort using balanced heaps, buildheap, max-heap removal for Θ(n log n) sorting, and its advantage in finding k largest elements and Kruskal's MST. Also introduces Binsort's basic idea of distributing items into piles by category before sorting each pile, illustrated with bill sorting.

nodes.title: 7.7 Binsort and Radix Sort
nodes.summary: The text covers Heapsort, its C++ implementation, time complexity, and advantage for finding k largest elements; Binsort and its extensions, including duplicate keys and large key ranges, limitations; Radix Sort with algorithm, example, complexity analysis, and optimization with large base; and introduces empirical comparison of sorting algorithms.

nodes.title: 7.8 An Empirical Comparison of Sorting Algorithms
nodes.summary: This section compares sorting algorithms empirically. It discusses Radix Sort's efficiency requirements and implementation challenges with real numbers and strings, questioning constant-time key comparison assumptions and analyzing Radix Sort's complexity. Empirical results for Insertion, Bubble, Selection, Shell, Merge, Quick, Heap, and Radix Sorts on various input sizes and orders are presented, highlighting optimized Quicksort's overall performance and Radix Sort's poor showing. It then introduces lower bounds for sorting, establishing that the problem is bounded by Ω(n) and O(n log n), and questions whether a faster general-purpose sorting algorithm might exist.

nodes.title: 7.9 Lower Bounds for Sorting
nodes.summary: The text covers empirical performance comparisons of sorting algorithms (O(n^2) sorts, Insertion Sort, Shellsort, optimized Quicksort, unoptimized Heapsort, Mergesort, Radix Sort) and the lower bound proof for comparison-based sorting. It introduces decision trees, proves an Ω(n log n) worst-case lower bound, explains its importance, discusses reductions, and notes Radix Sort's reliance on comparisons. Further reading on sorting and adaptive algorithms is mentioned, along with an exercise to prove Insertion Sort's correctness.

nodes.title: 7.10 Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text derives the Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison-based sorting using decision trees and Stirling's approximation, concluding Θ(n log n) time. It lists further reading: Knuth's definitive sorting reference, Sedgewick on Quicksort and algorithms, adaptive sorting, and a survey on adaptive algorithms. It ends with Exercise 7.1 asking to prove Insertion Sort correctness by induction.

nodes.title: 7.11 Exercises
nodes.summary: The text covers the lower bound proof that comparison-based sorting requires Ω(n log n) time, referencing decision trees, Stirling's approximation, and the Θ(n log n) complexity of sorting. It lists further reading on sorting, including works by Knuth, Sedgewick, and adaptive sorting, and provides exercises on proving Insertion Sort's correctness, analyzing Bubble Sort variations, stable sorting, Quicksort optimizations, SPLITk, nuts and bolts, small-set sorting, counting sort, searching lower bound, and Quicksort partition. It ends with a project on improving Bubble Sort with a flag.

nodes.title: 7.12 Projects
nodes.summary: This text covers internal sorting exercises and file processing. Section 7.12 projects include: determining which operations benefit from sorting; analyzing Mergesort with Insertion Sort thresholds; implementing Mergesort for linked lists; writing and analyzing counting sort; proving lower bounds for searching; and comparing Quicksort partition methods. Additional projects: optimizing Bubble Sort with a flag; explaining and implementing Double Insertion Sort; studying Shellsort increment schemes; comparing linked-list vs array Mergesort; optimizing Quicksort with pivot selection, insertion sort thresholds, and recursion elimination; optimizing Heapsort siftdown; implementing Radix Sort with bit shifting; and empirical comparisons of sorting algorithms. Chapter 8 introduces file processing and external sorting, covering primary vs secondary storage, disk drives, buffer pools, C++ random access, and external sorting principles.

This section covers internal sorting algorithms in main memory. It defines key terminology, notation, records, comparators, stability, and the sorting problem. It presents simple Θ(n²) algorithms (Insertion, Bubble, Selection Sort), Shellsort, and advanced Θ(n log n) algorithms like Mergesort, Quicksort, and Heapsort. Special-case Θ(n) sorting via Binsort and Radix Sort is discussed. Analysis includes average versus worst-case complexities, optimizations, and an empirical comparison. A lower bound proof establishes Ω(n log n) for comparison-based sorting. Further reading and exercises reinforce concepts, with projects for practical implementation and optimization.

nodes.title: 8 File Processing and External Sorting
8.1 Primary versus Secondary Storage
nodes.summary: This chapter covers file processing and external sorting, focusing on disk-based data. It contrasts primary (RAM) and secondary storage, highlighting cost, persistence, portability, and the million-to-one access time gap, which necessitates minimizing disk accesses via file structures and caching. It outlines disk drive architecture (platters, heads, arms) and direct access characteristics, then previews upcoming sections on disk drive physics, buffer pool management, C++ random access, and external sorting for data too large for memory, including a price comparison table for storage media.

nodes.title: 8.2 Disk Drives
8.2.1 Disk Drive Architecture
nodes.summary: The text covers disk drives and external sorting, focusing on caching, logical vs. physical files, and file manager roles. It details disk architecture: platters, read/write heads, tracks, cylinders, sectors, and zoned arrangements, contrasting with CD-ROMs. Disk access steps—seek, rotational delay, transfer—are explained, along with costs like track-to-track and average seek times. File organization concepts include clusters, extents, fragmentation, and internal fragmentation. It mentions File Allocation Tables, UNIX i-nodes, and sector headers with error detection. Tradeoffs between cluster size and performance are discussed, and an example provides disk drive specifications.

nodes.title: 8.2.2 Disk Access Costs
nodes.summary: This text covers disk sector structure with headers and gaps, then disk access costs including seek times, rotational latency, and transfer rates, illustrated by an example comparing sequential versus fragmented file reading. It discusses buffering and caching to minimize disk accesses, including sector-level buffering by OS and hardware, dual buffers for I/O, and the benefits of caching for performance, similar to CPU caches. It also explains why defragmentation improves file processing.

Section 8.2 covers disk drives and external sorting, including drive architecture, file organization, and access costs. It details platters, heads, tracks, cylinders, sectors, and zoned arrangements, contrasting with CD-ROMs. Disk access steps—seek, rotational delay, transfer—are explained with costs like track-to-track and average seek times. File organization concepts include clusters, extents, fragmentation, File Allocation Tables, UNIX i-nodes, and sector headers with error detection. Tradeoffs between cluster size and performance are discussed, with an example of drive specifications. Disk access costs include seek times, rotational latency, and transfer rates, illustrated by sequential versus fragmented file reading. Buffering, caching, dual buffers, and defragmentation benefits are covered.

nodes.title: 8.3 Buffers and Buffer Pools
nodes.summary: This text covers file processing and external sorting, focusing on buffers and buffer pools. It explains disk fragmentation, sector-level buffering, and double buffering to minimize disk I/O. It details buffer pool management with replacement strategies like FIFO, LFU, and LRU, including a virtual memory example. It discusses buffer pool ADTs: message-passing and buffer-passing styles, with examples, stale pointer issues, acquire/release mechanisms, and a revised buffer-passing ADT. Finally, it introduces the programmer's view of files in C++, including random vs. sequential access and the fstream class.

nodes.title: 8.4 The Programmer's View of Files
nodes.summary: The text covers buffer pool implementations using void* and the programmer's view of files, including the fstream class methods open, read, write, seekg, seekp, and close. It contrasts random and sequential file access, emphasizing that sequential access reduces I/O time when physical layout matches logical order. It then introduces external sorting for records too large for main memory, noting the need for disk I/O and the focus on single-disk-drive optimization, while contrasting it with internal sorting.

nodes.title: 8.5 External Sorting
8.5 External Sorting (intro)
nodes.summary: The text describes file I/O operations: read, write, seekg, seekp, and close, similar to a buffer pool ADT. It introduces external sorting for records too large for main memory, emphasizing minimizing disk I/O. It covers disk access modeling (blocks, sectors), the inefficiency of sequential processing on a single disk, and the key sort approach using an index file. Simple approaches like virtual memory and Quicksort are discussed, noting their limitations. The Mergesort-based external sort is outlined, including splitting into run files and merging runs with input/output buffers.

nodes.title: 8.5.1 Simple Approaches to External Sorting
nodes.summary: This text covers external sorting, focusing on simple virtual memory approaches, their limitations with large files and efficiency due to random access and log n I/O, and the superiority of external Mergesort. It details the basic Mergesort algorithm with sequential passes merging runs, doubling run length each pass, using double buffering across four disk drives. It explains reducing passes by creating larger initial runs via internal sorting of blocks, and mentions extending this with more memory and future topics: replacement selection for larger runs and multiway merging. Two core steps: break file into runs, then merge.

nodes.title: 8.5.2 Replacement Selection
nodes.summary: This text covers external sorting algorithms. It begins by explaining how the external mergesort algorithm improves performance by creating larger initial sorted runs using an internal sort, reducing passes. The replacement selection method is detailed, including its heap-based algorithm to generate runs on average twice the size of RAM, its step-by-step process, and a snowplow analogy to estimate run length. The section then introduces multiway merging to reduce merge passes by merging more than two runs simultaneously, better utilizing memory.

nodes.title: 8.5.3 Multiway Merging
nodes.summary: The text covers external sorting, focusing on the snowplow analogy for replacement selection, multiway merging to reduce merge passes, and examples of file sizes processable in one or two passes. It compares three external sort implementations (standard Mergesort, two-way Mergesort with large runs, and R-way Mergesort) via a table of time and block counts for various file sizes, concluding with guidelines: maximize initial run length, overlap I/O with processing, use more memory and disk drives. It also lists further reading on file processing, disk modeling, buffer management, and Knuth's snowplow argument.

Section 8.5 covers external sorting for large records, starting with file I/O operations and disk access modeling. It discusses simple approaches like virtual memory and Quicksort, highlighting their limitations, and introduces Mergesort-based external sorting with run creation and merging using input/output buffers and double buffering. Subsection 8.5.1 details simple approaches, the basic Mergesort algorithm, and reducing passes via larger initial runs. Subsection 8.5.2 explains replacement selection using a heap to generate runs twice RAM size, with a snowplow analogy. Subsection 8.5.3 covers multiway merging to reduce merge passes, compares three external sort implementations, and provides guidelines for optimization and further reading.

nodes.title: 8.6 Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text presents Figure 8.11 comparing three external sorting algorithms on small records, detailing time and blocks for various file sizes, with advice on using multiple disk drives. Section 8.6 lists further readings on file processing, external sorting, disk modeling, and buffer management. Section 8.7 provides exercises (8.1–8.7) on memory/storage pricing, disk drive specifications, and calculating read times for files under different storage layouts.

nodes.title: 8.7 Exercises
nodes.summary: This text presents exercises and projects for a chapter on file processing and external sorting. Exercises 8.1–8.13 involve calculating disk performance metrics (read times for files, tracks, sectors, bytes) using varied disk specifications from the 1990s to 2004, and comparing contiguous versus random storage. Exercise 8.14 asks for a proof about average track separation. Exercises 8.15–8.16 cover query processing algorithms and buffer pool replacement strategies (FIFO, LFU, LRU, MRU). Exercises 8.17–8.22 address replacement selection, multiway merge, sorting large databases, and variable-length records. Projects 8.1 examines performance improvements from faster CPU or disk.

nodes.title: 8.8 Projects
nodes.summary: The text presents external sorting exercises and projects: calculating largest mergeable file size, proving/disproving replacement selection sort condition, estimating sort time for ten million records, analyzing payroll scaling with CPU/disk/memory improvements, extending sorting to variable-length records, simulating buffer pool performance, comparing pixel packing, implementing LRU buffer pool and external sort, Quicksort with virtual array, and block vs. section merge I/O. It then introduces searching, defining exact-match and range queries, and categorizing algorithms into sequential/list, hashing, and tree indexing.

This section covers file processing and external sorting, focusing on disk-based data. It contrasts primary and secondary storage, details disk drive architecture and access costs (seek, rotational delay, transfer), and explains file organization (clusters, extents, i-nodes). Buffer pool management, including replacement strategies (FIFO, LFU, LRU) and ADTs, is discussed. The programmer's view of files via C++ fstream, with random and sequential access, is presented. External sorting techniques are detailed: simple approaches, Mergesort-based sorting with run creation and merging, replacement selection using heaps, and multiway merging. Comparative analysis of external sort implementations and optimization guidelines are provided. Further readings, exercises on disk performance and buffer replacement, and projects on external sorting and buffer pool simulation are included.

nodes.title: 9 Searching
9 Searching (intro)
nodes.summary: The text introduces searching as a core computing task for finding records by key. It defines formal search problem, successful/unsuccessful searches, exact-match and range queries. It categorizes search algorithms into sequential/list, hashing, and tree indexing, noting each suits the Dictionary ADT differently. It states Chapter 9 covers list-based methods (arrays/linked lists, sequences and sets, RAM), hashing (exact-match, no duplicates, RAM/disk), and Chapter 10 covers tree-based disk methods like B-trees. It then introduces sequential search on unsorted arrays with worst-case Θ(n), and begins analyzing average-case comparisons by considering probabilities of key positions and absence.

nodes.title: 9.1 Searching Unsorted and Sorted Arrays
nodes.summary: The chapter covers searching data in lists, focusing on arrays. It analyzes sequential search on unsorted lists, including average-case cost, then discusses sorted arrays and jump search, leading to binary search. It introduces dictionary/interpolation search and Quadratic Binary Search (QBS), analyzing QBS cost with Čebyšev’s inequality, comparing it to binary search in asymptotic and practical terms. The chapter notes hashing and B-trees for disk-based records, and begins Section 9.2 on self-organizing lists.

nodes.title: 9.2 Self-Organizing Lists
nodes.summary: The text covers self-organizing lists and bit vectors. It discusses practical limits of algorithm growth rates, comparing binary search and quadratic binary search (QBS) in comparisons and constant factors, noting QBS's dependence on data distribution. Self-organizing lists are introduced as an alternative to key-ordered lists, ordering by access frequency. It presents expected search cost formulas, examples with uniform and geometric distributions, and the 80/20 rule (Zipf distribution). Three heuristics—count, move-to-front, and transpose—are detailed with examples. Applications include data compression (move-to-front) and buffer pools. Finally, bit vectors for set representation are explained, including bitwise operations for union, intersection, and difference.

nodes.title: 9.3 Bit Vectors for Representing Sets
nodes.summary: The text explains bit vectors (bitmaps) for set representation, where a bit array marks set membership, enabling bitwise operations for union, intersection, and difference. It notes applications in document retrieval using signature files. It then introduces hashing for direct key-based access, defining hash functions, hash tables, and slots. Hashing is efficient for exact-match queries but unsuitable for range searches or ordered traversal. The section mentions hashing's use in databases alongside B-trees and provides a simple example, while noting potential inefficiencies.

nodes.title: 9.4 Hashing
9.4 Hashing (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers bit vector applications in document retrieval using signatures, then introduces hashing as direct-access searching. It defines hash functions, hash tables, slots, and collisions. The goal is mapping keys to slots for exact-match queries, noting hashing's unsuitability for range searches or ordered access. A simple example stores keys directly; a realistic example uses a larger key range than slots, causing collisions. The two-step search process is computing the hash and resolving collisions. Hash functions are discussed, with collisions nearly unavoidable, illustrated by the birthday problem. Perfect hashing, which eliminates collisions for a fixed set, is mentioned but costly, suitable for read-only databases.

nodes.title: 9.4.1 Hash Functions
nodes.summary: This section on hashing explains key concepts like hash functions, collisions, and collision resolution policies. It covers the need for hash functions when keys span a large range but the table is small, and discusses collision probability using the birthday paradox. It emphasizes the importance of good hash functions and the impact of key distribution, including natural frequency distributions, skewed data, and poorly distributed bits. It presents open hashing (separate chaining) and closed hashing (open addressing), detailing methods like linked lists for collision resolution, and provides examples of hash functions such as modulo, mid-square, string summing, and folding, noting the pitfalls of poor distribution and table size.

nodes.title: 9.4.2 Open Hashing
nodes.summary: Section 9.4.2 covers open hashing (separate chaining) using linked lists per slot, with insertion order, key order, or frequency order, and notes performance, clustering, memory suitability, disk issues, and Binsort similarity. Section 9.4.3 introduces closed hashing (open addressing) storing records in the table, and bucket hashing dividing slots into buckets with sequential search and overflow buckets.

nodes.title: 9.4.3 Closed Hashing
Bucket Hashing
nodes.summary: The text covers hashing techniques: open hashing performance (average Θ(1), clustering issue), its suitability for main memory, and similarities to Binsort. Closed hashing stores records directly, requiring collision resolution. Bucket hashing groups slots into buckets with overflow; search and insertion process, and a variant hashing to arbitrary slots. Bucket methods suit disk storage due to block-sized buckets and single disk access. Linear probing is introduced as closed hashing without bucketing, using a probe sequence for collision resolution.

nodes.title: Linear Probing
nodes.summary: The text covers hashing collision resolution: bucket hashing with overflow, where buckets have multiple slots, reducing initial collisions and optimizing disk access by reading whole buckets. It then details linear probing, explaining the probe sequence, insert/search routines using probe function p, and the requirement of an empty slot to avoid infinite loops. It illustrates linear probing's primary clustering problem, where clusters merge and cause unequal slot probabilities and long probe sequences, and suggests potentially skipping slots by a constant c, though with table size constraints.

nodes.title: Improved Collision Resolution Methods
nodes.summary: The text discusses collision resolution in hash tables, focusing on linear probing's primary clustering issue, where items cluster together, increasing probe sequence lengths. It presents improved methods: skipping slots by constant c, pseudo-random probing, quadratic probing (which can fail to visit all slots), and double hashing to avoid secondary clustering. It covers probe sequence properties, table size constraints (e.g., prime size), and examples. It concludes with analysis of closed hashing performance for insertion, deletion, and search, distinguishing successful and unsuccessful searches.

The section on closed hashing covers bucket hashing, where slots are grouped into buckets with overflow, suitable for disk storage due to block-sized access. It contrasts open hashing's performance and clustering issues. Linear probing is introduced for collision resolution, detailing probe sequences, insert/search routines, and the primary clustering problem. Improved methods are presented: skipping slots by constant c, pseudo-random probing, quadratic probing, and double hashing, along with probe sequence properties and table size constraints. The section concludes with performance analysis for insertion, deletion, and successful/unsuccessful searches.

nodes.title: 9.4.4 Analysis of Closed Hashing
nodes.summary: The text covers closed hashing collision resolution, focusing on double hashing to avoid secondary clustering, with an example and implementation considerations. It analyzes closed hashing performance using load factor, providing expected cost formulas for insertions, deletions, and searches, and notes linear probing's higher costs. It discusses efficiency trade-offs, recommending tables stay below half full, and mentions frequency-based record ordering. Finally, it addresses deletion using tombstones to maintain probe sequences and allow slot reuse, noting tombstone impact on probe distances.

nodes.title: 9.4.5 Deletion
nodes.summary: The text discusses hash table management, covering periodic rehashing to prioritize frequently accessed records and deletion handling. Deletion requires tombstones to avoid hindering searches and allow slot reuse, but tombstones increase average probe distances. Solutions include local reorganization upon deletion or periodic rehashing. It also lists further readings on self-organizing techniques, text compression, perfect hashing, collision resolution, document retrieval, and dynamic hashing. Finally, it introduces exercises, starting with expected cost versus unsuccessful search probability in sequential search.

Section 9.4 covers hashing for direct-access searching, defining hash functions, tables, slots, and collisions, with goals for exact-match queries and unsuitability for range searches. It introduces open hashing (separate chaining with linked lists) and closed hashing (open addressing, bucket hashing, linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing), discussing collision resolution, performance analysis, load factors, and deletion via tombstones. It includes hash function examples (modulo, mid-square, string summing, folding), the birthday problem, perfect hashing, rehashing, and further readings.

nodes.title: 9.5 Further Reading
nodes.summary: This text covers two solutions for mitigating performance degradation after deletions in hash tables: local reorganization by swapping records along probe sequences, and periodic rehashing to remove tombstones and optimize frequently accessed records. It then provides further reading on self-organizing techniques, text compression, Ziv-Lempel coding, self-organizing lists, Zipf distributions, document retrieval, perfect hashing, collision resolution analysis, and dynamic hashing. Finally, it introduces exercises, beginning with one on expected cost versus unsuccessful search probability for sequential search.

nodes.title: 9.6 Exercises
nodes.summary: This text from a data structures textbook covers deletion in hash tables, noting tombstones increase average path length and proposing local reorganization or periodic rehashing as solutions. It lists further readings on self-organizing lists, data compression, document retrieval, and perfect hashing. The exercises cover sequential and binary search cost analysis, interpolation search, selection algorithms, self-organizing list heuristics (count, move-to-front, transpose), bit vector set operations, birthday probabilities, hash function evaluation, closed hashing with linear, quadratic, and pseudo-random probing, string folding, double hashing, tombstone deletion, and primary clustering. The projects involve implementing and comparing search algorithms and self-organizing heuristics.

nodes.title: 9.7 Projects
nodes.summary: The text covers hash table exercises on sfold, double hashing with H1/H2, tombstone deletion, and pseudo-random probing permutation analysis. It lists projects: implement binary/quadratic binary search; compare self-organizing list heuristics; build text compression and document retrieval systems; create disk-based bucket hashing for a dictionary; and implement linear, quadratic, and pseudo-random probing for the dictionary ADT. It also introduces indexing for large disk-based datasets, covering entry-sequenced files, multiple search keys, and key-pointer indexing.

Chapter 9 covers searching algorithms for records by key, including sequential search on unsorted arrays, sorted arrays with jump, binary, interpolation, and quadratic binary search, comparing their costs. It examines self-organizing lists using count, move-to-front, and transpose heuristics, with applications like data compression and buffer pools. Bit vectors for set representation and operations are explained. Hashing is detailed with hash functions, open and closed hashing, collision resolution, performance, deletion strategies, perfect hashing, and rehashing. Further readings, exercises, and projects on implementing and comparing search algorithms, self-organizing heuristics, text compression, document retrieval, and disk-based indexing are provided.

nodes.title: 10 Indexing
10 Indexing (intro)
nodes.summary: The text introduces indexing for large disk-based datasets that exceed main memory, where hashing fails for range, ordered, or extreme-key queries. It defines entry-sequenced files, primary and secondary keys, and index files linking keys to records. It discusses linear indexing with sorted key/pointer pairs, fixed-length entries for variable-length records, binary search, and multi-level indexes for disk storage. It briefly outlines tree indexing, mentioning ISAM, 2-3 trees, B-trees, and B+-trees.

nodes.title: 10.1 Linear Indexing
nodes.summary: Section 10.1 covers linear indexing: sorted key/pointer pairs, fixed-length records pointing to variable-length database records, binary search benefits, and main-memory or disk storage. It describes two-level linear index for large indexes, update costs, duplicate key space waste, two-dimensional arrays, and inverted lists with linked-list implementations. Section 10.2 introduces ISAM as a modified linear index for large, frequently updated databases, noting its weaknesses that motivate B+-trees.

nodes.title: 10.2 ISAM
nodes.summary: The text covers indexing methods: inverted lists for secondary keys, detailing an array-based implementation with primary key pointers and combined lists, and its suitability for disk-based files. It introduces ISAM, an early disk-based method using sorted records, cylinders, in-memory tables, and overflow areas, noting its efficiency for static data but degradation with frequent updates, requiring periodic reorganization. Finally, it discusses tree-based indexing, including BSTs for primary and secondary keys, their efficiency in memory, but challenges on disk due to unbalance and disk I/O, leading to the need for better disk-based structures like B+-trees.

nodes.title: 10.3 Tree-based Indexing
nodes.summary: The text discusses limitations of linear indexing and ISAM for dynamic databases, then introduces tree-based indexing using binary search trees (BSTs) for large, frequently updated databases. It highlights BST challenges: unbalanced trees and disk I/O due to node placement across blocks, requiring balancing and block allocation strategies. It notes balancing costs during updates, referencing Figures 10.7 and 10.8. It then introduces 2-3 trees as height-balanced alternatives, describing their shape (nodes with 1-2 keys, internal nodes with 2-3 children, all leaves at same level) and search properties, with Figure 10.9 showing an example and Figure 10.10 an implementation. 2-3 trees lead to B-trees, the most widely used indexing method.

nodes.title: 10.4 2-3 Trees
nodes.summary: This text covers 2-3 trees, a height-balanced indexing structure. It defines their shape: nodes with one or two keys, internal nodes with two or three children, and all leaves at the same level. It describes the search tree property, node implementation, and search algorithm. Insertion is detailed, including simple insertion and node splitting with promotion, illustrated with examples and code. Deletion cases are briefly mentioned. Relationships between tree height and leaf count are derived, showing logarithmic time for operations. The section ends with an introduction to B-trees, noting their origin and widespread use.

nodes.title: 10.5 B-Trees
10.5 B-Trees (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers 2-3 tree insertion, including an example where root splitting increases tree height, and explains that insert/delete operations maintain height balance with all leaves at the same level, ensuring O(log n) operations. It introduces B-trees, their properties (height balanced, minimized disk I/O, linked records, minimum fullness), definition of order m, and search/insertion processes. It then describes B+-trees as a common variant where records are stored only in leaf nodes, internal nodes guide search, and leaf nodes are linked, managing a sorted array-based list in disk-block-sized chunks.

nodes.title: 10.5.1 B+-Trees
nodes.summary: The text covers B+-trees: their motivation as a common B-tree variant for disk-based systems, structural differences from B-trees (records only at leaves, linked leaves for range queries, internal placeholders), pseudocode for search, insertion, and deletion; split/merge/borrow rules and underflow handling; B*-trees with two-thirds full nodes; and analysis of asymptotic cost Θ(log n), high branching factors, shallow heights, storage utilization, and low internal-node overhead.

nodes.title: 10.5.2 B-Tree Analysis
nodes.summary: The text covers B*-tree splitting/merging rules, B-tree asymptotic analysis (Θ(log n) with high branching factors), practical shallow heights with examples, space efficiency from high fan-out, and reducing disk fetches via in-memory upper levels and buffer pools. It includes further reading references and two exercises on index capacity with specific disk block, key, and data sizes.

Section 10.5 covers B-trees and their variants. It introduces 2-3 tree insertion and height balance, then defines B-trees: height-balanced, minimized disk I/O, linked records, minimum fullness, order m, and search/insertion. B+-trees are detailed: records only in linked leaf nodes, internal placeholders, pseudocode for search, insertion, deletion, split/merge/borrow rules, underflow handling, and B*-trees with two-thirds full nodes. Analysis includes asymptotic cost Θ(log n), high branching factors, shallow heights, storage utilization, low internal-node overhead, reducing disk fetches via in-memory levels and buffer pools, plus further reading and exercises on index capacity.

nodes.title: 10.6 Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text discusses B-tree efficiency, noting that branched trees require minimal space for top levels and few disk fetches. Buffer pool management for B-tree nodes is covered, including LRU replacement and node locking, with modest pools often sufficient. Further reading cites works on file processing, primary/secondary indices, B-tree implementations, and buffer pool strategies. Exercises then pose problems on disk blocks, record storage, linear indices, second-level indices, and record packing for given key and data field sizes.

nodes.title: 10.7 Exercises
nodes.summary: The excerpt from Section 10.6 recommends further reading on file processing, indices, B-tree implementations, and buffer pool management. Section 10.7 provides sixteen exercises covering linear indices with disk blocks and key/data sizes, second-level indices, modifying binary search for variable-length records, constructing and improving inverted lists, comparing ISAM and B+-trees, proving 2-3 tree leaf counts, inserting into 2-3, 2-3+, B-, and B+-trees, deleting from B+-trees, and determining record capacity of B+-trees. Section 10.8 begins Project 10.1 on implementing a two-level linear index.

nodes.title: 10.8 Projects
nodes.summary: This text presents exercises and projects from a chapter on indexing. Exercises cover conditions for ISAM efficiency versus B+-trees, proving leaf node counts in 2-3 trees, and demonstrating insertions into 2-3, 2-3+, B-tree, and B+-tree structures. It includes inserting specific values and sequences of letter keys, deleting from a B+-tree, calculating minimum and maximum records for B+-trees of various heights, and lists projects: implementing a two-level linear index for variable-length records, implementing a 2-3+ tree, and implementing a dictionary ADT using a B+-tree with a buffer pool. The projects specify disk block sizes, record sizes, and node capacities.

Section 10 covers indexing for large disk-based datasets. It begins with linear indexing, using sorted key/pointer pairs and multi-level indexes, and inverted lists for secondary keys. ISAM is introduced for static data but degrades with updates. Tree-based indexing is then presented, starting with binary search trees and their disk I/O challenges, leading to 2-3 trees and B-trees. B+-trees are detailed with search, insertion, deletion, and variant B*-trees. Analysis includes logarithmic cost, high branching factors, and buffer pool management. The section ends with further reading, exercises, and projects on implementing linear indexes, 2-3+ trees, and a B+-tree dictionary.

summary: Part III covers sorting and searching. Chapter 7 details internal sorting: terminology, simple Θ(n²) algorithms, Shellsort, advanced Θ(n log n) algorithms (Mergesort, Quicksort, Heapsort), Binsort/Radix Sort, complexity analysis, and the Ω(n log n) lower bound. Chapter 8 addresses file processing and external sorting: disk architecture, access costs, file organization, buffer pool management, C++ file I/O, and external sorting techniques (simple, Mergesort-based, replacement selection, multiway merging). Chapter 9 explores searching: sequential, binary, interpolation, quadratic binary search, self-organizing lists, bit vectors, hashing (open/closed, collision resolution, perfect hashing), and related applications. Chapter 10 examines indexing for disk-based data: linear indexing, ISAM, binary search trees, 2-3 trees, B-trees, B+-trees, B*-trees, and performance analysis. Each chapter includes further readings, exercises, and projects.

nodes.title: 11 Graphs
11 Graphs (intro)
nodes.summary: This text introduces graphs, detailing their flexibility and applications like connectivity modeling, shortest routes, flow capacities, pathfinding, algorithm modeling, task ordering, and relationship modeling. It outlines chapters covering terminology, representations (adjacency matrix/list), graph ADT and implementations, traversal algorithms (DFS/BFS) with topological sorting, shortest route algorithms, and minimum-cost spanning tree algorithms. It defines graphs as G=(V,E), discussing sparse/dense/complete graphs, directed/undirected/labeled/weighted graphs, adjacency, paths, simple paths, cycles, and simple cycles. Figures illustrate graph examples and terminology.

nodes.title: 11.1 Terminology and Representations
nodes.summary: This text covers graph terminology, representations, and implementations. It defines vertices, edges, directed/undirected, labeled, weighted graphs, adjacency, paths, cycles, connectivity, subgraphs, connected components, acyclic graphs, and free trees. It describes adjacency matrix and adjacency list representations, including space requirements (Θ(|V|^2) vs. Θ(|V|+|E|)), trade-offs for sparse/dense graphs, and examples. It presents an abstract Graph ADT with methods for vertex/edge counts, weight, setEdge, delEdge, marks, and neighbor iteration (first/next), and discusses graph implementations.

nodes.title: 11.2 Graph Implementations
nodes.summary: This text covers graph implementations and traversals. It describes an abstract Graph ADT with fixed vertices, integer indices, methods for n, e, weight, setEdge, delEdge, getMark, setMark, first, next, and a traversal loop. It details adjacency matrix and adjacency list implementations, including edge storage, Mark array, and Edge class, with code examples. It then introduces graph traversals, contrasting them with tree traversals, and notes challenges like disconnected graphs and cycles.

nodes.title: 11.3 Graph Traversals
11.3 Graph Traversals (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers graph data structure implementations and traversals. It details an adjacency matrix class's edge methods (setEdge, delEdge, isEdge, weight, getMark, setMark). It introduces graph traversals, explaining their purpose, applications in AI, and challenges like disconnected graphs and cycles, solved via mark bits and a graphTraverse function. An adjacency list implementation (Graphl class) is provided, with methods for initialization, neighbors, edge operations, and marks. Finally, depth-first search (DFS) is described, including its recursive algorithm, use of a stack, construction of a DFS tree, and PreVisit/PostVisit hooks, applicable to directed and undirected graphs.

nodes.title: 11.3.1 Depth-First Search
nodes.summary: This section covers graph traversal algorithms using marked vertices to avoid cycles and ensure all components are visited via a wrapper function. It details Depth-First Search (DFS): recursive, stack-based, visits branches deeply, builds a DFS tree, and supports PreVisit/PostVisit actions, with cost Θ(|V|+|E|) for directed and undirected graphs. It also introduces Breadth-First Search (BFS), which uses a queue to visit vertices level by level. Finally, it introduces topological sort for scheduling tasks with prerequisites into a linear order.

nodes.title: 11.3.2 Breadth-First Search
nodes.summary: The text covers graph traversal algorithms from Chapter 11. It explains depth-first search (DFS), including preorder and postvisit actions, the visitor design pattern, and an example with a DFS tree, noting edge processing and cost Θ(|V| + |E|). It then introduces breadth-first search (BFS), which uses a queue instead of recursion, with example trees and processes. Finally, it introduces topological sort for scheduling tasks with prerequisites into a linear order. Figures 11.8-11.12 illustrate these concepts.

nodes.title: 11.3.3 Topological Sort
nodes.summary: This text covers graph traversals and shortest-path problems. It details depth-first search (DFS), including preorder/postorder processing and the visitor pattern, with an example and cost analysis. It introduces breadth-first search (BFS) using a queue, with implementation and example. Topological sort is explained for DAGs, both DFS-based and queue-based, with examples. Finally, shortest-paths problems are introduced, defining weighted directed graphs, path costs, and notation for shortest distances.

Section 11.3 covers graph traversals, starting with graph data structures like adjacency matrices and lists, and methods for edges and marks. It introduces traversal challenges such as cycles and disconnected graphs, solved with mark bits and a graphTraverse function. Depth-first search (DFS) is detailed with recursive stack-based algorithms, DFS trees, PreVisit/PostVisit hooks, and cost Θ(|V|+|E|). Breadth-first search (BFS) using a queue is explained with examples. Topological sort for DAGs is presented, both DFS-based and queue-based. The section concludes with an introduction to shortest-path problems in weighted directed graphs.

nodes.title: 11.4 Shortest-Paths Problems
nodes.summary: This text covers Section 11.4 on shortest-paths problems, including a queue-based topological sort algorithm, definitions of weighted graphs and shortest path concepts, and the single-source shortest paths problem. It explains Dijkstra's algorithm with an implementation, discusses two methods for finding the minimum-distance unvisited vertex (linear scan and priority queue), compares their time complexities for dense and sparse graphs, and provides a step-by-step illustration. It also briefly introduces Section 11.5 on minimum-cost spanning trees.

nodes.title: 11.5 Minimum-Cost Spanning Trees
11.5 Minimum-Cost Spanning Trees (intro)
nodes.summary: The text details implementing Dijkstra's algorithm using a min-heap priority queue for unprocessed vertices, including the DijkElem class and complexity trade-offs for sparse versus dense graphs. It provides code and a step-by-step example. It then introduces the minimum-cost spanning tree (MST) problem, its properties, and applications, and describes Prim's algorithm as similar to Dijkstra's but selecting the least-cost edge to any vertex in the MST, with a brief code comparison.

nodes.title: 11.5.1 Prim's Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text covers minimum-cost spanning trees (MSTs), including their definition, properties (no cycles, |V|-1 edges), and applications like wiring and telephone lines. It details Prim's algorithm with implementations using distance matrix and priority queue, and provides a proof of correctness using contradiction. An example of Prim's algorithm on a graph is given. It also introduces Kruskal's algorithm, which processes edges by weight and uses equivalence classes to build the MST.

nodes.title: 11.5.2 Kruskal's Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text covers Prim's minimum-cost spanning tree algorithm proof using marked and unmarked vertices with edge selection, illustrated by Example 11.3. It then introduces Kruskal's algorithm, its greedy approach using equivalence classes and edge processing, with Example 11.4. Implementation details include using a min-heap for edges and UNION/FIND for cycle detection, with worst-case and average-case time complexity analysis. Finally, it mentions further reading on Stanford Graphbase and lists exercises on graph edge counts and free tree properties.

This section covers minimum-cost spanning trees (MSTs), starting with Dijkstra's algorithm implementation using a min-heap priority queue, including the DijkElem class, complexity trade-offs, code, and an example. It then introduces the MST problem, its properties (no cycles, |V|-1 edges), and applications. Prim's algorithm is detailed with distance matrix and priority queue implementations, proof of correctness, and an example. Kruskal's algorithm is presented, using a greedy approach with equivalence classes, min-heap for edges, and UNION/FIND for cycle detection, along with complexity analysis. The section concludes with further reading and exercises.

nodes.title: 11.6 Further Reading
nodes.summary: Example 11.4 illustrates Kruskal's Algorithm steps on a graph: processing edges (C,D), (E,F), (C,F), rejecting (D,F), and accepting (B,C) and (A,C) into the MST. It mentions using a min-heap to process edges by weight, and the UNION/FIND algorithm for cycle detection. The implementation uses KruskalElem class. Complexity: worst-case Θ(|E| log |E|), often Θ(|V| log |E|) average. Section 11.6 references Stanford Graphbase. Section 11.7 exercises: prove max edges n(n-1)/2; prove connected acyclic graph has |V|-1 edges.

nodes.title: 11.7 Exercises
nodes.summary: This text covers Kruskal's MST algorithm steps, implementation, and complexity, including a code example. It discusses using a min-heap and UNION/FIND for efficiency, with worst-case Θ(|E| log |E|) and average-case Θ(|V| log |E|). It references further reading on the Stanford Graphbase. The exercises section includes proofs about graph edges, free trees, adjacency matrix and list representations, DFS and BFS trees, Dijkstra's algorithm, topological sort cycle detection, single-source and single-destination shortest paths, DAG root finding, longest path in DAG, cycle detection, Prim's and Kruskal's MST steps, maximum spanning tree, MST uniqueness and negative weights, Dijkstra's tree properties, bipartite graphs, and two-coloring trees. Projects cover graph file I/O, MST program, triangular adjacency matrix for undirected graphs, and performance comparison of Dijkstra implementations with different graph representations.

nodes.title: 11.8 Projects
nodes.summary: This text covers graph theory exercises and projects: spanning trees, MSTs, bipartite graphs, two-coloring, and algorithms for bipartite detection. Projects include file storage for graphs, MST programs, triangular matrix representation for undirected graphs, performance comparison of Dijkstra implementations, visitor pattern for DFS/BFS, and connected components labeling using UNION/FIND. It then introduces Chapter 12 on lists and arrays, covering multilists (lists with sublists), sparse matrices, and memory management, emphasizing logical versus physical representation.

Section 11 covers graph fundamentals: definitions, terminology, and representations (adjacency matrix/list). It presents the Graph ADT and implementations. Traversal algorithms DFS and BFS are detailed, including topological sort. Shortest-path problems, focusing on Dijkstra's algorithm with complexity trade-offs, are discussed. Minimum-cost spanning trees are covered via Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms, with proofs and complexity analysis. The section includes further reading, exercises on graph properties and algorithms, and projects like graph file I/O, MST programs, and performance comparisons. It concludes with an introduction to Chapter 12 on lists, arrays, and memory management.

nodes.title: 12 Lists and Arrays Revisited
12.1 Multilists
nodes.summary: Chapter 12 revisits lists and arrays, covering multilists (lists with sublists), including pure lists, reentrant lists, and cyclic lists, with representations like sequential arrays, linked lists with tag fields, and LISP-like linked nodes. It then discusses matrix representations for sparse matrices, such as lower triangular matrices and adjacency matrices for undirected graphs, and memory management techniques for allocating variable-length sections from a large array.

nodes.title: 12.2 Matrix Representations
nodes.summary: This text covers linked representations for lists and arrays, including pure and cyclic multilists with tag bits and pointers. It discusses matrix representations: lower and upper triangular matrices with index conversion formulas, and sparse matrices using hash tables, orthogonal lists, or Yale/Matlab formats, with space and time trade-offs. It also introduces memory management for variable-length records, highlighting pointer storage and disk considerations.

nodes.title: 12.3 Memory Management
12.3 Memory Management (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers sparse matrix representations, focusing on the Yale and Matlab formats, including storage details, access efficiency, and trade-offs. It then introduces memory management, defining the MemManager ADT with insert, get, and release operations, handles, and the concept of dynamic storage allocation. Examples include compiler runtime, OS memory, and disk file management. It discusses memory pools, allocation, deallocation, fragmentation, and the freelist for tracking free blocks.

nodes.title: 12.3.1 Dynamic Storage Allocation
12.3.1 Dynamic Storage Allocation (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers dynamic storage allocation, including managing memory blocks of variable sizes requested and released in any order, with examples like compiler runtimes, OS memory, and disk file managers. It defines 'heap' in this context, discusses the freelist, and explains internal and external fragmentation with illustrations. It describes sequential fit methods using doubly linked lists, approaches to implement the freelist (separate or borrowed space), and the structure of memory blocks with tags, size indicators, and pointers.

nodes.title: Sequential Fit Methods
nodes.summary: This text covers memory management from a chapter on lists and arrays. It details the structure of a doubly linked freelist and two approaches for storing it: separately or borrowing free block space. Sequential-fit methods—first fit, best fit, and worst fit—are explained with examples, noting their trade-offs and the need for block merging using tags and size fields. Buddy methods are introduced as an efficient alternative, using power-of-two block sizes, separate free lists, splitting on allocation, and simple merging with no overhead in reserved blocks.

nodes.title: Buddy Methods
nodes.summary: The text discusses memory management strategies: sequential-fit methods (best fit, worst fit, first fit) comparing their performance based on request patterns, and their limitations like O(n) search and merging complexity. It introduces the buddy system, which uses power-of-two block sizes, separate free lists, efficient splitting and merging using buddy addresses, solving many issues but causing internal fragmentation. An example and advantages/disadvantages are provided. Finally, other ad hoc approaches like dividing memory into zones with different management schemes (e.g., queues, freelists, general-purpose) are mentioned.

nodes.title: Other Memory Allocation Methods
nodes.summary: The buddy system's disadvantage is internal fragmentation, while its advantages include reduced external fragmentation, cheaper block search, and easy merging via buddy addresses differing by one bit; merging moves combined blocks to a larger freelist. Other memory allocation methods include dividing memory into zones with different schemes (e.g., queues, freelists), which can be efficient but risk poor zone sizing, and imposing standard sizes like clusters, leading to internal fragmentation but easier management and non-contiguous allocation. Failure policies for unserviceable requests include returning errors, compacting memory using handles for indirection, or deferring requests until memory is available.

nodes.title: Failure Policies and Garbage Collection
nodes.summary: Section 12.3 covers memory management. It discusses zone-based allocation and fixed-size block allocation, noting internal fragmentation but easier management and non-contiguous allocation, similar to disk clusters. Block management uses buffer pools. Section 12.3.2 addresses failure policies and garbage collection: when memory requests cannot be met, options include returning an error, compacting memory via handles for indirection, or deferring requests until memory is available.

Dynamic storage allocation manages variable-sized memory blocks requested and released in any order, as in compiler runtimes, OS memory, and disk file managers. It covers the heap, freelist, and internal/external fragmentation. Sequential fit methods (first fit, best fit, worst fit) using doubly linked freelists stored separately or in free blocks are explained with trade-offs and merging via tags and size fields. Buddy methods use power-of-two blocks, separate freelists, and easy splitting/merging, reducing external fragmentation but causing internal fragmentation. Other approaches include zone-based allocation and fixed-size blocks (like clusters), with failure policies such as errors, compaction via handles, or deferring requests. Garbage collection is also addressed.

nodes.title: 12.3.2 Failure Policies and Garbage Collection
nodes.summary: The text covers memory management approaches including zone and block allocation, internal fragmentation, and buffer pools. It discusses failure policies for unsatisfiable requests: error return, compaction with handles, deferred requests, and allocating more memory. Garbage collection is detailed: LISP and Java use it; reference counting has cycle issues, as in UNIX file systems; mark/sweep works but needs stack space, solved by the Deutsch-Schorr-Waite algorithm. Examples include LISP structures and memory leaks in C++.

nodes.title: 12.4 Further Reading
nodes.summary: Section 12.4 Further Reading lists references on LISP, Emacs, Java garbage collection, sparse matrix representations (Yale and MATLAB), and operating systems for memory management. nodes.title: 12.5 Exercises
nodes.summary: This text from a data structures textbook covers multilists with example figures and bracket notation exercises, references for Java garbage collection, sparse matrix representations (Yale and MATLAB), and memory management in operating systems. nodes.title: 12.6 Projects

It also includes projects to implement sparse matrix representations (orthogonal list, Yale model), memory managers (using separate or embedded free lists, buddy method), and garbage collection. It discusses matrix representations for sparse matrices, such as triangular matrices and orthogonal lists, with formats like Yale and Matlab. Memory management techniques are explored, including the MemManager ADT, dynamic storage allocation with heaps, freelists, and sequential fit methods (first, best, worst), buddy systems, and failure policies. nodes.title: 13 Advanced Tree Structures
13.1 Tries
nodes.summary: This chapter introduces advanced tree structures: tries for string storage using key space decomposition (including binary tries, alphabet tries, PATRICIA tries, and applications like DNA sequences); AVL trees and splay trees as self-balancing search trees with guaranteed performance regardless of insertion order; and spatial data structures organizing point data by xy-coordinates. It covers fundamental operations, implementation details left for projects, comparisons with BST object space decomposition, and discusses trie variants to avoid inefficiency.

nodes.title: 13.2 Balanced Trees
13.2 Balanced Trees (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers the PAT trie's search method, which compares one bit per internal node and one full key at the leaf, illustrated with DNA sequences. It then introduces balanced trees as a solution to BST imbalance, mentioning 2-3 trees and binary tries. The AVL tree is detailed: its balance property, O(log n) search and update, the four insertion imbalance cases, and rotations for rebalancing. The splay tree is briefly mentioned as a self-adjusting alternative.

nodes.title: 13.2.1 The AVL Tree
nodes.summary: Section 13.2 covers balanced trees, focusing on AVL and splay trees. It defines the AVL balance property, discusses insertion causing imbalance, and details four imbalance cases fixed by single or double rotations, with examples. It describes AVL insert and delete algorithms and analyzes O(log n) search and update times. For splay trees, it explains their goal of amortized O(log n) performance for sequences of operations, describes splaying via rotations to move accessed nodes to the root, and notes their self-organizing nature, without guaranteeing height balance.

nodes.title: 13.2.2 The Splay Tree
nodes.summary: The text covers balanced trees, focusing on AVL tree deletion and rotations, then introduces splay trees, explaining their operations (search, insert, delete) and splaying process with single, zigzag, and zigzig rotations, noting performance guarantees (O(m log n) for m operations) and lack of height balance. It includes examples of AVL and splay tree rotations. Finally, it transitions to spatial data structures, contrasting one-dimensional keys with multidimensional spatial attributes, and motivating spatial data structures for efficient range queries in geographic information systems, computer graphics, and robotics.

The section covers balanced trees beginning with PAT trie search operations and the need for balance in BSTs. It details AVL trees, including their balance property, O(log n) search/update, four insertion imbalance cases, and single/double rotations for insertion and deletion. Splay trees are introduced as self-adjusting alternatives with amortized O(log n) performance via splaying (single, zigzag, zigzig rotations), though without height balance. Examples of both AVL and splay rotations are provided. The section concludes by transitioning to spatial data structures, contrasting one-dimensional keys with multidimensional attributes and motivating efficient range queries for geographic information systems, computer graphics, and robotics.

nodes.title: 13.3 Spatial Data Structures
13.3 Spatial Data Structures (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers advanced tree structures, focusing on splay trees and spatial data structures. Example 13.4 details a search for 89 in a splay tree, requiring zigzig, zigzag, and single rotations to splay the found node to the root, making the tree shallower. Section 13.3 introduces spatial data structures for multidimensional keys, contrasting one-dimensional search trees. It discusses challenges with two-dimensional keys like coordinates, the need for efficient multidimensional range queries, and applications in GIS, graphics, and robotics. It outlines the k-d tree and PR quadtree, mentioning bintree and point quadtree variations, covering object vs. key space decomposition and binary vs. 2d-way branching. Section 13.3.1 describes the k-d tree as a BST extension with alternating discriminators, illustrating its use for 2D point storage.

nodes.title: 13.3.1 The K-D Tree
nodes.summary: This section covers spatial data structures for multidimensional point data, focusing on the k-d tree and PR quadtree. The k-d tree extends binary search trees using alternating discriminators per dimension, with details on search, insertion, deletion (using findmin), and range searching with Euclidean distance. The PR quadtree uses key-space decomposition with four-way branching in 2D. nodes.title: 14 Analysis Techniques
14 Analysis Techniques (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers analysis techniques for algorithms, emphasizing difficulties in modeling and solving equations. It highlights clever insights like the snowplow argument for Replacement Selection and contrasts with Quicksort's average-case analysis, where deriving a closed-form solution is hard. It mentions summations for iterative algorithms and recurrences for recursive algorithms, referencing Sections 14.1 and 14.2, which build on Section 2.4. Section 14.3 introduces amortized analysis, dealing with high-cost operations offset by lower subsequent costs, applied to UNION/FIND, Quicksort partition, splay trees, and self-organizing lists. Summation techniques are discussed, including induction, estimation, pairing, and guess-and-test with polynomial forms, illustrated by the sum of i from 1 to n yielding n(n+1)/2.

nodes.title: 14.1 Summation Techniques
nodes.summary: This text covers summation techniques and recurrence relations. For summations, it discusses estimating value, pairing terms, guess-and-test with polynomial assumptions and induction verification, and the shifting/subtract-and-guess method. Examples solve sum i, geometric series, and sum i2^i. For recurrence relations, it introduces using them to model recursive algorithm costs (e.g., Mergesort's T(n)=2T(n/2)+n) and briefly mentions three solving approaches: estimating bounds via induction, expanding to summation, and applying known theorems, with an example of guessing upper bounds for Mergesort.

nodes.title: 14.2 Recurrence Relations
14.2.1 Estimating Upper and Lower Bounds
nodes.summary: Section 14.2 covers recurrence relations, used to model recursive algorithm costs like Mergesort's T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. It outlines three solving approaches: estimating bounds via induction and tightening, expanding recurrences into summations, and applying known theorems for divide-and-conquer forms. Examples estimate Mergesort as Θ(n log n), compare factorial, 2^n, and n^n growth using logarithms, and analyze Fibonacci sequence growth as Θ(φ^n). It also introduces expanding recurrences for exact solutions.

nodes.title: 14.2.2 Expanding Recurrences
nodes.summary: The text covers analysis techniques for recurrence relations. It explains using the Fibonacci sequence to find the golden ratio φ and its exponential growth. It details expanding recurrences to find exact solutions, with examples for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 5n² and heap building cost. Finally, it introduces divide and conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + cn^k and begins deriving their general solution via expansion.

nodes.title: 14.2.3 Divide and Conquer Recurrences
nodes.summary: The text covers solving recurrences via expansion and the Master Theorem. It first derives the solution for f(n) ≤ 2f(n/2) + 2 log n, yielding 4n - 2 log n - 4. Then it introduces divide and conquer recurrences T(n) = aT(n/b) + cn^k, derives the general solution using expansion, analyzes cases based on r = b^k/a, and states the Master Theorem. Examples apply it to T(n)=3T(n/5)+8n^2 and Mergesort. Finally, it sets up the average-case recurrence for Quicksort and simplifies it.

nodes.title: 14.2.4 Average-Case Analysis of Quicksort
nodes.summary: The text covers the Master Theorem for solving recurrence relations, with examples for T(n)=3T(n/5)+8n^2 and Mergesort. It presents the average-case analysis of Quicksort, deriving its recurrence with full history and solving it using the shifting method to obtain Θ(n log n). Finally, it introduces amortized analysis, illustrating it with sequential searches in an unsorted array and binary counter increment, showing that the average cost per operation is constant despite worst-case costs.

Section 14.2 covers recurrence relations for analyzing recursive algorithms. It presents three solving approaches: estimating bounds via induction and tightening, expanding recurrences into summations for exact solutions, and applying the Master Theorem for divide-and-conquer forms. Examples include Mergesort's Θ(n log n), Fibonacci growth Θ(φ^n), and heap building. It derives solutions for recurrences like T(n) = aT(n/b) + cn^k, analyzes cases based on r = b^k/a, and states the Master Theorem. It applies the theorem to examples like T(n)=3T(n/5)+8n^2 and Mergesort, and sets up Quicksort's average-case recurrence, solving it to Θ(n log n). Finally, it introduces amortized analysis with examples of sequential search and binary counter increment.

nodes.title: 14.3 Amortized Analysis
nodes.summary: This section covers amortized analysis, which evaluates the total cost of a series of operations rather than individual worst-case costs. It illustrates amortized analysis through three examples: sequential searches in an unsorted array, incrementing a binary counter, and a stack with multipop operations. For multipop, the concept of potential is introduced to bound total cost. It also presents Theorem 14.2, proving that move-to-front self-organizing lists incur at most twice the comparisons of an optimal static ordering, with a detailed proof. The section concludes with further reading references and exercises on solving summations using polynomial guessing and other techniques.

nodes.title: 14.4 Further Reading
nodes.summary: This text covers a comparison of move-to-front and optimal static ordering, noting move-to-front requires fewer than twice the comparisons. It lists further reading on recurrence relations, amortized analysis, splay trees, and self-organizing sequential search heuristics, citing works by Roberts, Graham et al., Cormen et al., Sleator and Tarjan, and Bentley and McGeoch. It also presents four exercises: solving summations of i^2, i^3, a general range sum of i^2, and the sum of i/2^i using techniques like guessing polynomials, subtract-and-guess, and divide-and-guess.

nodes.title: 15 Lower Bounds
15 Lower Bounds (intro)
nodes.summary: Chapter 15 covers lower bounds for problems, defining upper and lower bounds and their importance in algorithm analysis. It reviews lower bounds for sorting, searching unordered and ordered lists, and finding the maximum value, using models like partially ordered sets and adversarial proofs. It introduces state space lower bounds, presents a linear-time worst-case algorithm for finding the ith largest element, and discusses sorting with minimal comparisons. Section 15.1 explains that a good algorithm's upper bound matches the problem's lower bound, noting that even when bounds meet, new algorithms like Quicksort can offer practical benefits.

nodes.title: 15.1 Introduction to Lower Bounds Proofs
nodes.summary: The text covers lower bounds proofs in algorithms: adversarial proofs, state space bounds, and examples like finding the ith largest element and sorting comparisons. It introduces lower bounds as the tightest bound for all algorithms, discusses matching upper and lower bounds for algorithm quality, and presents a design algorithm. Using maximum finding and Towers of Hanoi, it illustrates achieving optimality. Lower bounds for searching lists, including unsorted lists with unique keys and comparison-based search, are analyzed, with Theorem 15.1 stating an n-comparison lower bound for unsorted search.

nodes.title: 15.2 Lower Bounds on Searching Lists
nodes.summary: The text covers lower bounds proofs, starting with the Towers of Hanoi optimality and variations. It then addresses searching: unsorted lists, proving n comparisons are needed via flawed attempts and a partial order proof; sorted lists, using decision trees to show binary search is optimal in worst and average cases, with exceptions like interpolation search and sorting costs. Finally, it introduces finding the maximum value in an unsorted list, presenting a simple algorithm requiring n comparisons and questioning its optimality.

nodes.title: 15.3 Finding the Maximum Value
nodes.summary: Section 15.3 covers proving optimality of binary search and finding the maximum in an unsorted list. It discusses average case analysis, including the Harmonic series and variance. It presents a flawed proof for the maximum, then a correct comparison-based proof using posets. Section 15.4 introduces adversarial lower bounds for finding the second largest, critiques a flawed proof, and explores divide-and-conquer algorithms.

nodes.title: 15.4 Adversarial Lower Bounds Proofs
nodes.summary: The text covers lower bounds proofs for finding the second largest and the minimum/maximum. It critiques a flawed 2n-3 proof, presents divide-and-conquer algorithms, and introduces binomial trees and adversary arguments to achieve optimal n + ceil(log n) - 2 comparisons for second largest. It then addresses finding both minimum and maximum, showing a divide-and-conquer recurrence with costs ranging from 3n/2-2 to 5n/3-2 depending on division.

nodes.title: 15.5 State Space Lower Bounds Proofs
nodes.summary: Section 15.5 covers state space lower bounds for finding minimum and maximum, proving optimality via adversary arguments and poset analysis, with recurrences and divide-and-conquer strategies like splitting into sizes 2 and n-2. Section 15.6 introduces finding the ith best element, focusing on the median, using a poset model that requires only i-1 smaller and n-i larger elements, and suggests adapting Quicksort's partitioning to solve it faster than sorting.

nodes.title: 15.6 Finding the ith Best Element
nodes.summary: Section 15.6 covers finding the ith best element, starting with the minimum information needed (i-1 smaller, n-i larger) and the lower bound of n + ceil(n/2) - 2 comparisons. It discusses using Quicksort-like partitioning for median finding, with average O(n) but worst-case O(n^2). It then presents a worst-case linear-time algorithm using medians of groups of five, with recurrence analysis showing T(n) ≤ 23n for n ≥ 380, though impractical due to high constants. Section 15.7 introduces optimal sorting, aiming for the fewest comparisons, analogizing to sports tournaments.

nodes.title: 15.7 Optimal Sorting
nodes.summary: Sec. 15.7 covers optimal sorting, analyzing median selection recursion for linear time, proving T(n) ≤ 23n for n ≥ 380, but noting impracticality due to high constants. It then explores minimum-comparison sorting, comparing to sports tournaments, introducing binary insert sort, merge insert sort (Ford-Johnson), and its near-optimality, discussing information-theoretic lower bounds (log n!), S(n) optimal worst cost, and cases like n=12 where lower bound is underestimated (30 comparisons). Sec. 15.8 mentions further reading on lower bounds. Sec. 15.9 begins exercises on algorithm definitions and tournament scheduling.

nodes.title: 15.8 Further Reading

Section 15.9 presents exercises: 15.1 questions if the 'algorithm for algorithms' is truly an algorithm or a heuristic, referencing Section 1.4; 15.2 introduces scheduling difficulties in single-elimination tournaments for n basketball teams, with n = 2^i. The preceding text includes Figure 15.7 on merge-insert sort for ten elements, discusses optimal worst-case cost S(n), bounds S(n+1) ≤ S(n) + ceil(log(n+1)), S(n+m) ≤ S(n) + S(m) + M(m,n), and notes merge sort is not optimal but nearly optimal for small n, with n=47 example splitting into 5 and 42.

nodes.title: 15.9 Exercises

nodes.title: 16.1.1 The Knapsack Problem

nodes.title: 16.1.2 All-Pairs Shortest Paths
nodes.summary: This text covers dynamic programming algorithms. It explains the Knapsack problem's recurrence and an example with a table showing solutions. nodes.title: 16.3 Numerical Algorithms
