It then introduces numerical algorithms for large values where hardware operations are insufficient, defining input size as the log of the value and discussing cost implications. Specific algorithms covered include exponentiation via divide-and-conquer (Power function, recurrence, and cost analysis) and Euclid's algorithm for largest common factor based on the property that common divisors divide differences.

nodes.title: 16.3.1 Exponentiation
nodes.summary: The text covers numerical algorithms, noting there are 2^k instances of length k or less, size of n is log n, and algorithm cost varies with n's length. It details exponentiation via a divide-and-conquer recursive Power function, with recurrence f(n) = f(⌊n/2⌋) + 1 + n mod 2 and solution f(n) = ⌊log n⌋ + β(n) − 1, requiring log n multiplications, exponentially better than n−1. It also introduces Euclid's algorithm for largest common factor, based on the property that if k divides n and m, then k divides n−m, leading to LCF(n, m) = LCF(n−m, n) = LCF(m, n−m) = LCF(m, n).

nodes.title: 16.3.2 Largest Common Factor
nodes.summary: The text covers numerical algorithms, discussing algorithm cost relative to input length and the relationship between value and size. It details exponentiation using a divide-and-conquer approach with its recurrence relation and cost analysis, showing improvement over naive multiplication. It presents Euclid's algorithm for finding the largest common factor, including its derivation and O(log n) complexity. Finally, it introduces matrix multiplication, noting the standard Θ(n³) algorithm and mentioning Strassen's algorithm as a faster alternative.

nodes.title: 16.3.3 Matrix Multiplication
nodes.summary: The text explains the LCF algorithm using the property LCF(n,m)=LCF(m,n mod m), with recursive code and O(log n) cost proof. It covers standard matrix multiplication at Θ(n^3) and Strassen's algorithm using seven multiplications and 18 additions, achieving Θ(n^2.81) but with higher constants. It discusses pseudorandom sequences, unpredictability, equidistribution, and the Linear Congruential Method using a seed and formula r(i) = (r(i-1) × b) mod t, noting thermal noise alternatives.

nodes.title: 16.3.4 Random Numbers

It then covers random numbers, including properties of randomness, pseudorandom sequences, and the Linear Congruential Method (LCM) with seed, constants, modulus, cycle length, and example with t=13 showing varying b values. It provides a specific LCM formula. Finally, it introduces the Fast Fourier Transform by noting multiplication complexity O(n²) vs addition O(n), and logarithm properties enabling multiplication via addition, as in slide rules.

nodes.title: 16.3.5 The Fast Fourier Transform

It explains linear congruential generators, emphasizing the importance of choosing good parameters for cycle length, with examples. It then introduces FFT, starting from multiplication via logarithms and slide rules, and details polynomial evaluation, interpolation, and roots of unity. The Discrete Fourier Transform matrix and inverse are defined, and the recursive FFT algorithm is given for efficient polynomial multiplication in Θ(n log n) time. The section ends with further reading and exercises on dynamic programming, Floyd's algorithm, and skip lists.

nodes.title: 17 Limits to Computation

nodes.title: 17.1 Reductions

nodes.title: 17.2 Hard Problems
17.2 Hard Problems (intro)

nodes.title: 17.2.1 The Theory of NP-Completeness
nodes.summary: Section 17.2 defines hard algorithms as exponential time and introduces NP-completeness. It explains non-determinism, the class NP, and contrasts problems like Towers of Hanoi with TRAVELING SALESMAN. It defines decision problems, NP-hard, and NP-complete, using TRAVELING SALESMAN and K-CLIQUE. The section discusses the significance of NP-completeness, the P=NP question, and the class P. nodes.title: 17.2.2 NP-Completeness Proofs
nodes.summary: This text covers NP-completeness: defining NP-hard and NP-complete, explaining that a polynomial-time solution for Traveling Salesman would imply P=NP, and outlining Cook's proof that SAT is NP-complete. It details reductions, especially SAT to 3-SAT and K-CLIQUE to VERTEX COVER, and provides a direct SAT to K-CLIQUE reduction. It then discusses coping with NP-complete problems via small instances, pseudo-polynomial algorithms like Knapsack, and special cases such as bipartite graphs or 2-SAT.

nodes.title: 17.2.3 Coping with NP-Complete Problems
nodes.summary: The text covers coping with NP-complete problems: running small instances, pseudo-polynomial algorithms (Knapsack), solving restricted cases (bipartite graphs, 2-SAT, small dimensions), dynamic programming, backtracking, branch-and-bound, and approximation heuristics (TSP, Vertex Cover, Bin Packing with first-fit and decreasing first-fit guarantees).
